We cannot see the air.

titlePageNarration.text: How Can a Bone Move?
Kit bends his arm. His hand moves toward his shoulder. How can stiff bones let that happen?
Bones meet at the elbow. The joint lets them change angle without bending the long bones themselves.
Strong bands called tendons join muscles to bones. A muscle can pull on a bone through these bands.
A muscle at the front of the upper arm shortens. It pulls the forearm closer to the shoulder.
The elbow bends. The upper arm bone and forearm bones stay firm while their positions change.
To straighten the elbow, muscles at the back of the upper arm pull. The front muscles relax.
Muscles pull bones. They do not push bones back. Different muscles can pull the joint in different directions.
Kit bends, then straightens his arm. Pulling muscles move the bones around the elbow joint.

Some lake water changes into water vapor. This gas mixes with the air. We cannot see the vapor.

titlePageNarration.text: A Hedgehog in Winter
A European hedgehog hunts in the fall. Cold weather is coming, and its small prey will become harder to find.
The hedgehog eats and builds fat inside its body. That stored fat can supply energy later.
It gathers dry leaves into a sheltered nest. The thick leaf walls help protect it from sudden changes in temperature.

Warmer spring days arrive. Small prey become easier to find. The hedgehog spends more time moving and feeding again.

titlePageNarration.text: The Long Hand Goes Around
The long hand points to twelve. Later, it points there again. Is the time still the same?
At three o’clock, the short hand points to three. The long hand is the minute hand. It starts at twelve.
Fifteen minutes pass. The long hand reaches three. The short hand has moved a little beyond three too.
After thirty minutes, the long hand reaches six. The short hand sits halfway between three and four.
After forty-five minutes, the long hand reaches nine. The short hand is closer to four now.
The long hand reaches twelve again. It has made one full turn. Sixty minutes have passed: one hour.
Look at the short hand. It points to four now. The long hand’s place matches the start, but the time does not.
The long hand returns to twelve after one hour. The short hand now points to four, showing the later time.

titlePageNarration.text: A Rocket Pushes Up
A rocket waits on the launch pad. Hot gas bursts from its engine. What can lift this heavy machine?
This rocket carries fuel and liquid oxygen. Inside the engine, they react and make very hot gas.
The engine pushes gas through a shaped opening called a nozzle. The gas rushes downward.
As gas goes down, it pushes the rocket up. This upward push is called thrust.
Earth’s gravity still pulls downward. When the upward push is strong enough, the rocket lifts away from the pad.
High above Earth, there is very little air. The rocket carries its own oxygen, so its engine can still work.
Gas shoots backward from the engine. The rocket receives a push forward, even without ground or air behind it.
The rocket moves one way as it sends gas the other way. The escaping gas makes the push.

titlePageNarration.text: Where Does My Heart Send Blood?
Zoe feels a beat inside her chest. Her heart is a muscle that squeezes to push blood along.
Blood travels through blood vessels. These branching tubes reach all around the body.
Blood returning from the body first reaches the right side of the heart. It needs more oxygen.
That side pumps blood toward the lungs. When we breathe in, fresh air enters the lungs too.
In the lungs, oxygen moves from the air into the blood. Blood carries this oxygen away.
The blood returns to the left side of the heart. Now the heart sends it out toward the body.
Tiny vessels bring blood close to body cells. Oxygen leaves the blood and helps those cells do their work.
Blood also carries carbon dioxide away from the cells. This waste gas will travel back to the lungs.
The blood returns to the heart, then reaches the lungs again. Carbon dioxide leaves the blood, and we breathe it out.
Heart to lungs, back to heart, then around the body: blood keeps moving through these connected routes.

titlePageNarration.text: Why Does Wind Blow?
The windsock points inland. Air is moving from the sea toward the beach. Moving air is wind.
Why is the air moving this way? On this sunny day, the land warms faster than the nearby sea.
The warm ground heats the air above it. The sea keeps the air near its surface cooler.
As air warms, it spreads out. The same amount of air takes up more room.
The warmer air is less dense than cooler air nearby. It can rise above that cooler air.
Cooler air near the sea moves inland. It pushes beneath the warmer air and helps lift it.
Higher above the coast, air moves back toward the sea. The air follows a larger turning route.
Farther over the water, cooler air sinks. This helps complete the moving-air loop.
Other weather can change this breeze. Wind does not always blow toward land whenever the Sun shines.
Here, uneven warming helped start a sea breeze. The windsock stretches inland as the cooler air passes.

A little robot rolls toward a foam block. It has no human eyes, but it has a touch sensor.
The sensor sits behind the front bumper. When something presses the bumper, the sensor detects that push.
The robot reaches the block. Its bumper presses inward, and the sensor sends a message to the controller.
The controller runs a program. This program says what the robot should do when the bumper is pressed.

Next, the wheels turn backward. The robot moves away, and the bumper springs out again.
Then the robot turns and rolls along a clear path. Its sensor helped trigger these actions.
Zoe moves the block into the new path. This robot uses its bumper each time it meets an obstacle.
When its bumper touches again, the same program runs: stop, move back, then turn.
The sensor reports a push. The program gives the next steps. Together, they help this robot change its route.

titlePageNarration.text: From Rice Field to Bowl
A bowl of rice begins with a plant. The grains grow in clusters near the tops of its stems.
When this crop is ready, a machine cuts the stems and collects the grain.
The grain must be separated from the stems. This step is called threshing.
Fresh grain holds moisture. Drying removes some water so the grain can be stored with less risk of spoilage.
Each grain still has a tough outer husk. We do not cook and eat that covering.
At the mill, a machine removes the husk. The grain underneath is brown rice.
To make white rice, milling also removes much of the brown outer layer. The grain looks paler now.
Workers sort and pack the rice. A bag can now travel to a shop and then a kitchen.
An adult cooks the rice with water. The grains take in water and become softer.
Plant, grain, husk removed, then cooking: the rice in this bowl has changed at each step.

titlePageNarration.text: A Satellite Keeps Going
A satellite travels high above Earth. It keeps moving around our planet instead of dropping straight to the ground.
Earth's gravity still pulls the satellite. Being in space does not make that pull disappear.
A rocket gave the satellite speed before letting it go. The satellite keeps moving forward after that.
Without Earth's pull, it would continue along a straight path. But gravity keeps changing the direction of its travel.
The satellite moves forward while falling toward Earth. Below it, Earth's surface curves away.
With the right speed and height, it keeps missing the ground. Its curved path goes around the planet.
That path is an orbit. The satellite is falling around Earth, not floating where gravity cannot reach it.
Different satellites use different orbits. Some travel close to Earth, while others travel much farther away.
Engineers choose a path for the satellite's job. They also plan ways to adjust it when needed.
Forward motion and Earth's pull keep this satellite following a curved route. Around Earth it goes again.

titlePageNarration.text: How Do We Choose a Ride?
On this practice map, the museum stands across a river. Kit and Zoe compare three ways to get there.
They could walk over the footbridge. The whole walk would take twenty-five minutes.
The bus must use the road bridge. Its route goes farther upstream before crossing the river.
The bus ride takes fifteen minutes. That sounds quicker, but the ride is only part of the journey.
They must also walk for ten minutes altogether and wait ten minutes. The bus journey takes thirty-five minutes.
The ferry has a shorter crossing. Its ride takes only five minutes, but they must check its waiting time too.
Here, walking takes five minutes altogether, waiting takes ten, and the ride takes five. The ferry journey takes twenty minutes.
Twenty minutes is less than twenty-five or thirty-five. For this trip, the ferry gives them the quickest whole journey.
On another day, a longer wait could change their choice. They would need to check the times again.
They choose the ferry for this practice trip. They have compared the walking, waiting and riding before deciding.

titlePageNarration.text: Messages Through My Body
Kit rolls a ball toward Zoe. She sees it coming and reaches to stop it. What helps her do that?
Light from the ball reaches Zoe's eyes. Cells inside her eyes respond to the light.
Messages travel from her eyes along nerves to her brain. These messages help her see where the ball is.
Her brain uses this information as she decides to stop the ball. Then it sends messages toward her arm muscles.
The messages pass down her spinal cord and along nerves into her arms. This route connects brain and muscles.
Her muscles pull on bones to move her arms and hands. Zoe reaches in front of the rolling ball.
The ball touches her fingers. Cells in her skin respond to the pressure and send more messages along nerves.
Those messages help her brain know that her hands have reached the ball. She can adjust her grip.
Nerve cells pass messages to other nerve cells. Many connections help the body keep sensing and moving.
Zoe holds the ball still. Messages helped her see it, reach for it and feel it in her hands.

titlePageNarration.text: When the Ground Shakes
During an earthquake, the ground shakes. The shaking can begin when rock suddenly slips along a break below the surface.
Earth's outer shell is divided into huge plates. These plates move very slowly, carrying rock with them.
Here, rock on opposite sides of a fault is moving in different directions. A fault is a break where rock can slip.
Rough surfaces can catch against each other. Part of the fault stays stuck while the surrounding rock keeps being pushed.
The rock slowly changes shape under that push. Energy builds up while the stuck part holds.
When the push becomes strong enough, the stuck part slips. Rock on the two sides moves suddenly.
Energy spreads outward as earthquake waves. The waves travel through rock and can reach the ground above.
As waves pass, the ground moves back and forth or up and down. That motion is the shaking people feel.
A wave carries energy away from the slipping rock. The whole block does not travel along with each wave.
Slow movement can build strain. A sudden slip releases it, sending waves through the ground. That is how this earthquake begins.

titlePageNarration.text: How Wings Lift a Plane
A plane is heavy, yet its wings help hold it in the air. What are the wings doing?
As the plane moves forward, air flows around its wings. Both the upper and lower wing surfaces affect that moving air.
The wings turn some of the flowing air downward. In return, the air pushes upward on the wings.
This upward part of the air's force is called lift. Most lift on this plane comes from its wings.
Air pressure also helps us describe that force. Air pushes on every side of the wing, but not equally.
For this lifting wing, the combined pressure pushes more upward than downward. That difference produces lift.
Pressure differences and air turning happen together. They describe the same lift, not two separate forces to add.
Gravity pulls the plane downward. In steady, level flight, lift balances the plane's weight.
Wing shape, speed and angle all affect lift. Pilots change how the plane flies as it takes off or lands.
The plane keeps moving through air. Its wings change the airflow, and the air's force helps support the plane.

titlePageNarration.text: A Message Crosses the Internet
Zoe sends Kit a picture of her paper boat. Their devices are in different homes. How does the picture reach his screen?
The picture is stored as data. The device can turn that data into signals that other equipment can carry.
The data travels in small groups called packets. Each packet has information that helps it reach the right destination.
Zoe's tablet uses Wi-Fi to send signals to a nearby router. This first part of the route uses radio waves.
The router connects to the internet provider's network. From there, other routers pass the packets onward through connected links.
In this example, the packets reach a messaging service's server. This computer helps deliver the picture to Kit.
Packets can follow different routes through a network. The receiving equipment uses their information to put the data together correctly.
The data reaches Kit's home network. His router sends signals to his laptop over Wi-Fi.
His laptop uses the received data to show the picture. The red boat appears on his screen.
The picture crossed many connections as coded data. Screens, routers, cables and radio signals helped it reach Kit.

titlePageNarration.text: From Cotton to Shirt
This shirt began with cotton plants. Inside their ripe, open bolls, soft fibers grew around the seeds.
After harvest, a machine called a gin separates the fibers from the seeds. The fibers are pressed into large bales.
At a mill, machines clean the fibers and line them up. They form a soft, loose strand.
Spinning twists the fibers together into yarn. Many short fibers can now hold together as one much longer strand.
A loom weaves yarn into fabric. One set of yarns crosses over and under another set.
The woven cloth is treated and colored. This cloth becomes pale blue before workers cut the shirt pieces.
Workers cut pieces for the front, back and sleeves. Their shapes must fit together when the shirt is sewn.
A sewing machine joins the pieces with thread. Seams hold the sleeves and body together.
Workers add the collar and buttons. The flat pieces now make a shirt that someone can put on.
Cotton fibers became yarn, yarn became cloth, and cut cloth became a shirt. Its fabric still contains those plant fibers.

titlePageNarration.text: Light in the Rainforest
Sunlight reaches the top of this rainforest. Far below, the ground is much darker. What happens to the light on its way?
The upper branches spread many leaves across the sky. Together, this leafy layer forms much of the canopy.
Leaves absorb some sunlight and reflect some away. Much less light passes through to the plants below.
Green leaves use light to help make food from water and a gas in the air. This process supports the growing tree.
Some of the tree's food helps it grow fruit. A toucan can feed on that fruit high in the branches.
Below the canopy, scattered patches of sunlight reach the ground. Many young plants grow in the dimmer light between them.
Some plants can live with little light. Others need more light to grow well. The forest does not suit every plant equally.
When a large tree falls, it can leave a gap overhead. More sunlight reaches the ground through that opening.
Young trees in the gap may grow faster with more light. As branches fill the space, shade can return below.
The rainforest changes from bright treetops to shaded ground. Where light reaches leaves helps shape what can grow and feed there.

titlePageNarration.text: One Shirt, Two Washdays
A museum washboard helps us explore an older way to wash. Its ridged board and hand-turned rollers each have a job.
In our demonstration, an adult washes a yellow shirt with water and soap. The cloth moves against the board's ridges.
The rubbing helps loosen dirt from the cloth. Clean rinse water then carries away soap and loosened dirt.
Next, the adult turns the wringer's handle. Its two rollers squeeze extra water from the wet shirt.
The shirt is still damp after wringing. It goes on a line to dry before someone wears it again.
On a later washday, the same shirt goes into an automatic washer. This time, a motor does much of the moving.
Inside, the drum turns the clothes through water and detergent. This movement helps clean them without rubbing each piece by hand.
The machine rinses the clothes and drains the water. Then a fast spin removes much of the water left in the cloth.
The shirt still needs to dry. The tools have changed, but cleaning, rinsing and removing extra water remain part of washday.
This is one comparison of two methods. People still wash in different ways, using the water, tools and power available to them.

titlePageNarration.text: When a Reef Gets Too Warm
This coral looks like a rocky mound, but tiny animals cover its surface. They are called coral polyps.
The polyps make a hard skeleton beneath their living tissue. Tiny algae live inside that tissue in many reef-building corals.
The algae use sunlight to make food. They share some with the coral, which gives them a protected place to live.
These algae also give much of the coral its color. Food from the algae helps this coral grow.
If the surrounding water stays too warm, the coral can become stressed. Then it may lose its algae.
The coral loses many of its algae. With fewer algae inside, its living tissue becomes much less colorful.
The white skeleton shows through the pale tissue. This change is called bleaching. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead.
Without enough algae, the coral loses a major food supply. If the stress lasts too long, the coral can die.
If conditions improve in time, algae can increase again. Some corals recover their color and continue growing.
Warm water can make this coral lose algae and turn white. If the heat eases, the living coral may recover.
